title: Why God forbade the earnings of prostitution from entering His house, the danger of trying to sanctify sin with an offering, and the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
paragraphs: Why God forbade the earnings of prostitution from entering His house, the danger of trying to sanctify sin with an offering, and the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing at the entrance of God's house, holding money earned through a life you desperately wish you could escape.
Your hands are trembling.

You have heard that God receives offerings. You have heard that He is merciful. Perhaps somewhere deep inside, you believe that giving Him a portion of what you earned might silence your guilt, cleanse your conscience, or make you worthy of His attention.
But then you encounter a command in Scripture that stops you cold.
“Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog, into the house of the LORD thy God for any vow: for even both these are abomination unto the LORD thy God.”
— Deuteronomy 23:18, KJV
Why would a merciful God refuse such an offering?
Was He disgusted by the woman?
Was her past too filthy for His presence?
Was her soul beyond redemption?
Or was God exposing something far more disturbing—something that even respectable, religious, churchgoing people continue doing today?
What if the real scandal is not simply the sin committed outside God's house, but the attempt to make that sin acceptable inside it?
To understand this passage, we must resist the temptation to read it through modern assumptions and return to the original language and covenant context in which it was written.
Deuteronomy 23:17–18 contains several significant Hebrew expressions. In the Hebrew Bible, these verses are numbered 23:18–19.

The preceding verse uses the words קְדֵשָׁה (qĕdēšāh) and קָדֵשׁ (qādēš), traditionally understood as referring to female and male cult prostitutes or persons associated with prohibited religious practices.
Both terms are linguistically related to the Hebrew root קדשׁ (q-d-sh), associated with holiness, consecration, or being set apart.

The precise historical functions of these individuals remain debated among biblical scholars, particularly regarding institutionalized temple prostitution. Nevertheless, the passage clearly prohibits these practices among Israel.
There is a disturbing irony here.
Something associated with religious consecration could nevertheless be forbidden by the very God whose holiness Israel was commanded to reflect.
Not everything called sacred is holy.
Not everything performed in the name of worship honors God.
Not everything offered at an altar is acceptable to the One being worshiped.
The next verse begins:
לֹא־תָבִיא אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה וּמְחִיר כֶּלֶב בֵּית יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ
Lō-tāḇî ʾeṯnan zônāh ûmĕḥîr keleḇ bêṯ YHWH ʾĕlōheḵā.
A close rendering of this portion is:
“You shall not bring the payment of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the LORD your God.”
The Hebrew expression אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה (ʾeṯnan zônāh) refers to the payment or earnings of a prostitute.
The expression מְחִיר כֶּלֶב (mĕḥîr keleḇ) literally means “the price of a dog.”

Some interpreters understand “dog” here as a derogatory expression for a male prostitute, particularly because of the preceding verse. Others understand it literally or propose different associations. The exact meaning is disputed, and intellectual honesty requires that we acknowledge this rather than present an interpretation as an undisputed translation.
The passage also contains the word תּוֹעֵבָה (tôʿēḇāh), commonly translated as “abomination” or something detestable.
God was establishing a boundary between practices He prohibited and the worship offered in His name.
Israel was not permitted to take these proceeds and present them in fulfillment of a sacred vow, as though bringing them into the sanctuary could make their origin acceptable.
The altar was never intended to become a place where disobedience could be disguised as devotion.
And suddenly, this ancient command becomes painfully relevant.
Because prostitution is not the only sin human beings have attempted to dress in religious clothing.
What about the businessman who cheats his employees but gives generously to the church?
The corrupt official who steals from the poor but sponsors religious celebrations?
The employer who withholds fair wages while proudly displaying Bible verses in the office?
The person who destroys another person's reputation on Saturday and raises both hands in worship on Sunday?
The religious leader who exploits vulnerable people and then calls the proceeds a blessing from God?
The believer who thinks that giving money can compensate for refusing to repent?
We may never have earned money through prostitution.
But have we ever tried to purchase peace with God while protecting something He has commanded us to surrender?
Have we ever used generosity to silence conviction?
Have we ever confused religious activity with genuine transformation?
The prophet Isaiah confronted a people who continued offering sacrifices while practicing injustice.
“Bring no more vain oblations.”
— Isaiah 1:13
God instructed them instead to cease doing evil, learn to do good, seek justice, and defend the vulnerable (Isaiah 1:16–17).
Through Amos, God rejected religious celebrations that existed alongside injustice, declaring:
“But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.”
— Amos 5:24
And Proverbs 21:27 declares that the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination, especially when brought with an evil intention.
The message is consistent.
God is not impressed by the size of an offering when the heart offering it refuses His correction.
He cannot be bribed.
He cannot be manipulated.
He cannot be persuaded to call darkness light simply because darkness has donated something to a religious institution.
But here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Because some people will read Deuteronomy 23 and conclude that a woman with a sexually broken past is permanently unwelcome before God.
That conclusion would miss the breathtaking testimony of the Gospel.
God's rejection of a prohibited offering is not a declaration that the person who earned it is beyond redemption.
There is a difference between refusing to sanctify sin and refusing to save a sinner.
Jesus Christ makes that distinction unmistakably clear.
Consider Rahab.
Scripture identifies her as a prostitute living in Jericho (Joshua 2:1).
She was not introduced to us as a woman with an impressive religious background. She did not possess a spotless reputation.
Yet when she heard what the God of Israel had done, she responded in faith.
She confessed that the LORD was God in heaven above and on earth beneath (Joshua 2:11).
Hebrews 11:31 remembers her faith.
James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of that faith.
And Matthew 1:5 records her name in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Read that again.
A woman remembered for prostitution appears in the earthly family line of the Messiah.
The Bible does not celebrate her prostitution.
It celebrates the faith through which she became part of a story greater than her past.
What society might have considered a permanent stain did not prevent God from incorporating her into His redemptive purposes.
Not because sin became acceptable.
But because God's grace was greater than her history.
Then we encounter Jesus in Matthew 21:31–32, speaking to religious leaders.
His words must have been deeply unsettling:
“The publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.”
The Greek word translated as “harlots” is πόρναι (pornai), referring to prostitutes.
Jesus was not declaring prostitution righteous.
He explained that tax collectors and prostitutes believed John's message, while the religious leaders, despite witnessing their response, refused to believe.
The scandal was not that Jesus welcomed repentant sinners.
The scandal was that people who considered themselves righteous could remain so hardened that they refused the very mercy those sinners were receiving.
A broken person who recognizes the need for grace is in a profoundly different spiritual position from someone who hides behind religious respectability and refuses to repent.
Perhaps that is why this passage hurts.
Because we prefer to identify with the people standing inside the sanctuary.
We rarely imagine ourselves as the ones standing outside, trembling, ashamed, and desperate for mercy.
Yet Romans 3:23 leaves none of us untouched:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
The preacher.
The prostitute.
The wealthy donor.
The struggling believer.
The religious scholar.
The person reading this article.
The person writing it.
Every one of us needs a Savior.
And perhaps someone reading these words right now has been carrying a secret that nobody knows.
Perhaps your past includes sexual sin.
Perhaps you survived through choices you now regret.
Perhaps you were manipulated, trafficked, exploited, or forced into circumstances you never chose.
Please understand that being abused or coerced is not the same as willingly committing the wrongdoing of those who exploited you. Their violence is not your moral guilt.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that God sees you only through the worst thing you have done—or the worst thing someone has done to you.
But the Gospel does not tell wounded people to purchase their way back into God's presence.
It points them to Jesus.
Consider the unnamed woman in Luke 7:36–50.
Scripture describes her as a sinner, although it does not specifically identify her as a prostitute.
She entered a Pharisee's house, stood behind Jesus, wept at His feet, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them.
The Pharisee saw her reputation.
Jesus saw the woman before Him and exposed the Pharisee's lack of love.
The story ends with words that no amount of money could purchase:
“Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.”
— Luke 7:50
Imagine hearing those words after years of believing that shame would be your permanent identity.
Go in peace.
Not go and purchase your forgiveness.
Not go and prove that you deserve mercy.
Not go and become respectable enough for Me to love you.
Your faith has saved you.
Go in peace.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
We do not bring an offering to purchase redemption.
Christ offered Himself to accomplish redemption.
First Peter 1:18–19 reminds us that we were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
The Greek word ἐλυτρώθητε (elytrōthēte) means “you were redeemed” or “you were ransomed.”
Our redemption was accomplished at a cost we could never pay.
The cross declares both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable depth of divine mercy.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because we could not save ourselves from it.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are proclaimed to those who repent and believe.
That is why grace must never become an excuse to continue exploiting others.
When Zacchaeus encountered Jesus in Luke 19, his response included generosity toward the poor and a commitment to repay those he had defrauded.
He did not attempt to erase injustice by making a religious donation while keeping everything else unchanged.
His encounter with Christ produced a different relationship with money, possessions, and the people he had harmed.
Genuine repentance does not ask, “How much must I give so that God will overlook what I am doing?”
It asks, “Lord, what must change now that I belong to You?”
Sometimes repentance means returning what was stolen.
Sometimes it means ending a dishonest business practice.
Sometimes it means confessing a hidden sin.
Sometimes it means seeking help to escape exploitation.
Sometimes it means admitting that the money we proudly called a blessing came at someone else's expense.
And sometimes the most meaningful offering begins not with opening our wallets, but with opening the parts of our hearts we have kept locked against God.
Psalm 51:17 says:
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”
A contrite heart.
A heart no longer defending its rebellion.
A heart that stops negotiating with God.
A heart that says, “Jesus, I cannot rewrite my past, but I surrender my future to You.”

You do not need to reveal your private struggles to strangers. God already knows them. But perhaps those simple words will encourage another person who has been silently wrestling with the same conviction.
Because in Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is also why Christian giving must flow from a heart transformed by grace.
The apostle Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 9:7
The Greek expression ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) means “a cheerful giver.”
Not a frightened giver.
Not a manipulated giver.
Not someone attempting to purchase God's approval.
A person whose generosity flows from a willing heart.

Scripture also teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and Paul gratefully acknowledges the Philippians' partnership in his ministry (Philippians 4:15–18).
Supporting Gospel-centered work can therefore be a meaningful expression of Christian stewardship.
And this is where I want to extend a personal invitation to you.
If you desire to glorify God through the resources He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting this ministry could be one expression of that desire.
It is not a payment for God's blessings, a required biblical tithe, or a condition of His love.
It is an opportunity to help continue and expand a mission dedicated to bringing biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the message of redemption to more people.
Because somewhere beyond your screen, someone may be wondering whether God could ever forgive them.
Someone is drowning in guilt.
Someone has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Someone has forgotten what Scripture actually teaches.
Someone believes their scandal has permanently erased their future.
And a message that takes you only a few minutes to read could become the encouragement that leads someone else to open their Bible, seek help, pray again, or turn toward Jesus.
These benefits are our way of thanking those who choose to stand alongside this mission.
But the greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is helping more people encounter biblical truth in a world overflowing with spiritual confusion.
It is reminding the broken that Jesus Christ still saves, forgives, restores, and transforms.
Your willingness to place biblical truth before your own community can greatly help this ministry reach people beyond its existing audience.
Never underestimate what God can accomplish through a truth faithfully shared.
But before you leave, return with me to that trembling person standing at the entrance of God's house.
The offering is in their hands.
The shame is in their heart.
The past feels unbearable.
They have nothing with which to purchase forgiveness.
Nothing with which to negotiate innocence.
Nothing with which to erase yesterday.
And then comes the message of the cross.
Jesus Christ has accomplished what silver and gold could never accomplish.
The invitation is not to make sin respectable.
It is to repent, believe, receive mercy, and walk in newness of life.
Deuteronomy teaches us that prohibited earnings cannot be made holy merely by bringing them into God's house.
The Gospel teaches us that sinners can be forgiven and transformed through Jesus Christ.
There is no contradiction.
The same God who refuses to call sin holy is the God who provides redemption for sinners.
He does not need to compromise His holiness to demonstrate His mercy.
At the cross, righteousness and grace meet without either being abandoned.
And that is why your past does not have to own you forever.
First Corinthians 6:11 contains one of the most beautiful declarations in Scripture:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
Such were some of you.
Were.
There is an entire testimony hidden inside that little word.
There is a former identity that no longer has the final authority.
There is a history that grace has not denied, but redemption has overcome.
There is a future that sin does not have the right to dictate.
You cannot buy that transformation.
You cannot earn that forgiveness.
You cannot donate your way into eternal life.
But you can come to Christ in repentance and faith, trusting the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
God refused to let sinful earnings purchase a place at His altar—but Jesus gave His own life so that sinners could find their way home.
